content: 1. The safety and efficacy of extended-release tablets in children under 16 years of age have not been established. 2. Avoid or use alternative drugs when combining clavulanate and pexidartinib, as both can increase toxicity. Pexidartinib is known to cause hepatotoxicity, and coadministration with other hepatotoxic agents should be avoided. 3. Pretomanid regimens are associated with hepatotoxicity. Avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic agents, including herbal supplements and drugs other than bedaquiline and linezolid. 4. When combining clavulanate and mipomersen, use caution and monitor liver function tests (LFTs), as both drugs have the potential to increase hepatic enzymes. 5. Medications that may cause hepatotoxicity, such as valoctocogene roxaparvovec, can increase the risk of elevated liver enzymes when combined with other hepatotoxic agents. Monitor closely and consider alternative medications to avoid potential drug interactions. 6. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. These reactions are more likely in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens. If an allergic reaction occurs, discontinue treatment immediately and initiate appropriate therapy. 7. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs), such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), may occur. If a skin rash develops, monitor closely and discontinue treatment if lesions progress. 8. Ampicillin-class antibiotics are excreted in human milk. While caution should be exercised when administering to nursing mothers, the drug may be used during lactation. Trace amounts in breast milk may pose a risk of sensitization but are not known to have detrimental effects on the breastfed infant. 9. Use caution in patients with hepatic impairment, as hepatic dysfunction is more common in elderly individuals, males, and those undergoing prolonged therapy. Hepatic dysfunction may occur even after completing therapy. 10. A high percentage of patients with mononucleosis develop a rash during therapy with ampicillin-class antibiotics. These antibiotics are not recommended for such patients. 11. Extended-release tablets are not interchangeable with other formulations due to differences in the amoxicillin-to-clavulanate ratio. They are also not recommended for use in patients with severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30 mL/min). 12. The incidence of diarrhea is higher with amoxicillin-clavulanate than with amoxicillin alone. 13. There is a risk of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) with antibiotic use. If CDAD is suspected, discontinue the drug immediately and provide appropriate fluid/electrolyte therapy, protein supplementation, and C. difficile-specific antibiotic treatment. 14. Prescribing antibiotics in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of drug-resistant bacteria. 15. Reproductive studies in animals have shown no teratogenic effects. However, in a study involving women with preterm premature rupture of the fetal membrane (pPROM), prophylactic treatment with this drug was associated with an increased risk of necrotizing enterocolitis in neonates. Use during pregnancy should be avoided unless deemed essential by the physician. 16. The drug is widely distributed in the body, except in the central nervous system (CNS). It is partially metabolized by the liver and primarily excreted unchanged in the urine. 17. Patients undergoing hemodialysis or with severe renal impairment should not use extended-release formulations. 18.
